national.title: Ground stop shows "we have to get off old network," Duffy says
national.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that "we have to get off old network, old telecom" after a telecommunication outage led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
national.body: Washington — Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "we have to get off old network, old telecom" after a telecommunication outage that officials said stemmed from overloaded routers prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. "For decades, this work in the FAA has not been done. It hasn't been done because it's hard," Duffy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."The ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers, creating chaos in the nation's airports at the start of the weekend. Officials said that FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies had performed maintenance updates at a remote facility to replace aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. And as the router was being switched, it started flooding other routers and overloaded the system.Duffy said the FAA is looking into why, when it conducted the installation in El Dorado, Arkansas, it started to broadcast data, but also why a second issue occurred at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, where work had been conducted weeks earlier. He said along with L3Harris, which operates and owns the network, the FAA is on site and the FBI is offering support. "We're looking at that right now, and when we know what the root cause of this issue was — was it the install from L3Harris, was it the router — I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find," he said. Duffy said for the telecom in El Dorado, it was an old copper wire that had become unusable. He said, "We were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work. And that's when we saw the flooding of the network.""So this is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network," Duffy said.The transportation secretary said the work was done "appropriately," noting that it's been done thousands of times and "this has never happened." He explained that normally, work is done on big facilities overnight. But for remote locations, that work can be conducted during the day, "Because the risk, historically, has been very low.""Obviously, on Friday we saw no; it flooded our network, and we had to take the extraordinary step of issuing a ground stop," he said. national.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as company conducts internal probe over Nvidia fallout
national.summary: Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.
national.body:
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence." It did not address specific allegations.

"The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," it said in an emailed statement.

Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company," the statement said. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters."

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was "no evidence" of illicit chip transfers.

national.title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
national.summary: Protesters say the move will stifle media freedom, while the coalition government insists broadcasters need to cut costs.
national.body:
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the license fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44, £7.06) a month for Czech TV and Czech radio.

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence in 1993.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

national.title: Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop and demands more money from Congress
national.summary: The president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.
national.body:
Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America's air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs." The Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration as part of the party's sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as an down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden's administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, to "upgrade the foundation" of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Duffy was the administration's public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.

national.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on D.C. public golf course redevelopment
national.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."

The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."

The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue," it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."

national.title: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course on Sunday
national.summary: The temporary order is part of a months-long challenge to the US president's plans to upgrade East Potomac Golf Links into a championship course.
national.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".

"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

national.title: The Reader: A new review source for book lovers
national.summary: With most newspapers and wire services closing the book on sections devoted to book reviews, Washington Monthly introduces its new online resource, offering reviews, essays, and recommendations by some of the world's top writers.
national.body: It's become an all-too-familiar story: Earlier this year, the Washington Post put an end to Book World, its weekly book review supplement. "Books are expensive," said bestselling author Jonathan Alter. "Readers need help to know what's good out there." Alter says Book World's closure created a void: "Thirty years ago, there were 30 American newspapers that, as part of their Sunday newspaper, had a book review section," he said. Today, only The New York Times still maintains a separate book review section. "So, we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it," said Alter, who is co-founder of The Reader, a new, general interest, online book review, to be published every weekday. Executive editor Haley Sweetland Edwards said, "We will have mostly book reviews, but also essays about books, columns about the literary book world, and top authors like Robert Caro and Margaret Atwood and Ann Patchett will be providing recommendations of books that have slipped below the cultural radar." The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine. Edwards says authors lined up to be part of it: "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize-winners who have agreed to be contributors over the next year. These are the crème de la crème, and they will be reviewing for us." Alter said, "We will review books that are going to become big bestsellers, but we're also going to review those books that sometimes fly under the radar, that are really good and that just aren't getting the recognition that they deserve." And that's where "Sunday Morning" comes in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration – one fiction, one non-fiction – courtesy of The Reader. national.summary: In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks about his characterization in the documentary "You Can See Everything," as well as threats he says have been made against his family's safety.
national.body: Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview. Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'""You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it. "I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. national.summary: The Korean-American novelist and bestselling author of "Pachinko" talks about her latest book, "American Hagwon," part of her series chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.
national.body: It's been nearly a decade since Min Jin Lee's last book made her a literary phenomenon. "Pachinko," a sweeping historical epic chronicling four generations of a Korean family living in Japan, sold more than two million copies in the United States. It was adapted into a popular series on Apple TV.But all that success didn't come easily. "When 'Pachinko' first came out as a hardcover, it was never on the bestseller lists," said Lee. "If you look at my hardcover sales, they're abysmal. So, if you start out with failure, it's really easy."Did she consider "Pachinko" at its beginning a failure? "Oh, I think you can ask my publishers!" she laughed. "They would just say, this didn't sell!"It wasn't until The New York Times named it one of the best books of the year, and it was selected as a National Book Award finalist, that "Pachinko" took off. Lee's latest novel, "American Hagwon" (published by Cardinal), is the third in a series she calls "The Diaspora Quartet," chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world."Every industrial revolution had people leaving the farm to go to the city," Lee said. "And now we have environmental diaspora, where people don't have water in their communities anymore. You have economic diaspora, where certain jobs don't exist anymore, like manufacturing. I'm focusing on Koreans, because those are the people that I know about. But I'm really writing about this modern condition."It's a deeply personal story for Lee. She came to America in 1976, when she was seven years old. The middle of three girls, her family moved to Elmhurst, Queens, where she grew up in a very blue-collar neighborhood. national.title: Flights expected to normalize by tonight after ground stop. Here's what to know
national.summary: Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
national.body: Air travel should resume normal operations by Sunday night after a rare national ground stop lasted more than four hours on Friday, causing chaos in the nation's airports as thousands of flights were canceled and travelers were stranded.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that travelers should expect delays to continue but "we should be running at full capacity" heading into Monday."What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way," he said.More than 1,400 flights are canceled for Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 2,200 others are delayed. How did the FAA ground stop happen?The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. ET Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air."The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday.This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country. national.title: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
national.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack.
national.body:
An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.

US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.

Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.

As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.

According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

national.title: New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision
national.summary: The lawsuit filed by New Orleans officials also requests that the tanker involved in the collision with the cruise ship be seized and sold to pay for damages.
national.body:
The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of a tanker that crashed into a cruise ship docked there on Friday.

The port is claiming the tanker is at fault for the collision that saw more than 100 passengers being rescued from the Mississippi River and caused more than $1m (£756,000) in damage, according to court documents.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.

The court documents added that the port terminal had been "significantly damaged" in the incident.

The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd are all named in the lawsuit filed in federal court on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana.

Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover clean-up, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

national.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
national.summary: It marks the second attack on the country in three days and comes as the US and Iran remain locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.
national.body:
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

national.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
national.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.
national.body:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".

The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.

national.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
national.summary: The film Being Heumann tells the lesser-known story of the mother of the disability rights movement. A new generation of activists share how they "carry the torch" today.
national.body:
Andrew Pilkington, Siena Rafter, Charlie Rush-Reese, Dylan O'Brien, Roberta Colindrez, Ruth Madeley and Madeline Delp in Being Heumann , premiering November 13, 2026 on Apple TV. Apple TV hide caption

Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.

Being Heumann , the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Sian Heder , tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.

Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 . It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.

But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

national.body:
Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat, during a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese.

About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, located in a remote part of the Andes mountains of northern Peru, but the Pope's visit still drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.

At an outdoor Mass, the Pope spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages" and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.

More than 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.

Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.

In his sermon, the Pope thanked those who had made the journey to see him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.

The pontiff's Latin America tour comes roughly a month after he underwent surgery to remove part of his right lung after a cancerous lump was found during routine checks.

At the start of his trip, he said the care he had received made him think of those who "lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment for health conditions.

national.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base

national.body:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month.

Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October.

Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts."

The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total.

Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.

Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.

Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.

national.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
national.summary: Both Hamas and IDF officials confirm the death of Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade.
national.body:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

national.title: Copper wire upgrade behind US flight suspension, transport secretary says
national.summary: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.
national.body:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said.

Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment.

Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights.

Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment.

Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said.

The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued."

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds.

The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.

national.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
national.summary: A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House.
national.body:
Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."

The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."

national.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
national.summary: Some college football games were delayed a few hours on Saturday or postponed to Sunday. And in Oklahoma at least, there will be perks for fans to make up for the inconvenience, including cheap beers.
national.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings , will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference . The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

local.body: Travelers at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport faced another day of delays and cancellations following a nationwide ground stop Friday that disrupted thousands of flights across the country.Among them was 5½-year-old Esakhan and his family, who were visiting relatives in Toronto and trying to return home to Atlanta.“Our flight got canceled yesterday and it was still canceled today,” Esakhan said.WATCH: 'Our flight got canceled': Travelers at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport facing cancellations, delaysHis mother said they were told their flight was delayed because of a shortage of flight attendants. “We're just hoping that our flight gets here soon and then we can leave,” she said.Across the country, more than 12,500 flights have been canceled since the FAA grounded virtually all flights for four hours Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on outdated technology that became overloaded.Flights have since resumed at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport, but many passengers were still dealing with the ripple effects.Kyle Johansen of Lockport said he and his wife were supposed to fly through Atlanta to Fort Lauderdale.“Now our Fort Lauderdale flight has been canceled and we're going to miss our cruise ship,” Johansen said.Another traveler headed back home New Orleans said he spent the night at the airport after his plans were disrupted, sleeping on a couch in the terminal.Other travelers faced hours-long delays. One couple said they were originally supposed to arrive in Phoenix at 6:30 p.m. but were now expecting to get there around 11:30 p.m.Another couple said they were told there was roughly a 50-50 chance their flight would leave after an additional three-hour delay. local.title: Senator seeks to overturn Freedom Tax Credit opt-in
local.summary: State Democrats’ newly restored veto-proof supermajority may get a test next year over New York’s opt-in to President Donald Trump’s Education Freedom Tax Credit program. Gov. Kathy Hochul opted into the program in October, joining several other states. Not all Democrats in the state Legislature are
local.body:
State Democrats' newly restored veto-proof supermajority may get a test next year over New York's opt-in to President Donald Trump's Education Freedom Tax Credit program.

Gov. Kathy Hochul opted into the program in October, joining several other states. Not all Democrats in the state Legislature are happy with the move, however, including Sen. John Liu, D-Bayside. Liu recently introduced S.10734, which would amend the state Education Law to designate the state Board of Regents as the sole entity responsible for determining whether New York state will participate in the program as well as requiring the Board of Regents to determine and submit the state’s list of qualified scholarship granting organizations to the federal government.

If passed, Liu's legislation would give the Board of Regents the authority on an annual basis to decide whether New York would participate in the voucher program beginning with the 2028 tax year. Liu had opposed the program before Hochul opted New York into the program.

"However the Trump administration may spin it, this tax credit is a federal voucher program, an idea long debated and rejected in the state of New York because it inevitably diverts resources away from public schools. Though public schools may receive some of the donations eligible to be refunded as tax credits, the clear intent is to subsidize private schools, with the public education funding already cut by the administration. New York should not buy into this terrible policy, advanced by a now lame-duck administration, which has some likelihood of being reversed in the near future," Liu said. "Regardless of what the political arguments may be, this program is a matter of education policy best decided by the state Board of Regents which for over 200 years has set policy for all schools in New York State in a manner largely shielded from the prevailing politics of the times. This legislation appropriately places this matter in the hands of the Board of Regents."

Nearly all schoolchildren in at least 30 states can apply for a new federal scholarship next year to help pay for private school, homeschooling and other educational expenses, according to regulations proposed Thursday by the Trump administration.

The first national school choice scholarship program, the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, will launch Jan. 1, establishing a taxpayer-funded incentive for families to choose private or homeschooling in participating states. Taxpayers who donate to an organization passing out the scholarships will receive a federal tax credit, a perk expected to further fuel the conservative school choice movement. Taxpayers will have the chance to donate to a scholarship program in a participating state, even if they do not live there, starting Jan. 1. Individuals can donate up to $1,700 and receive a federal tax credit for the same amount in exchange. Federal officials propose a couple filing jointly could give as much as double that amount. Scholarship organizations in each state would decide how much to grant to each child who applies, depending on available funds and student need. Children could qualify if they are in elementary through high school and their families earn up to three times the area's median income. For a family of four in Houston, for example, that equates to more than $300,000.

local.title: Centaur Stride needs succession plan to keep riding
local.summary: They say the only two certainties in life are death and taxes. The difference is that we know exactly when our taxes are due. The timing of the other is never quite so certain. Perhaps the best we can do is make the most of the time we have: play the cards we are dealt, […]
local.body:
They say the only two certainties in life are death and taxes. The difference is that we know exactly when our taxes are due. The timing of the other is never quite so certain.

Perhaps the best we can do is make the most of the time we have: play the cards we are dealt, make changes where we can, and leave things a little better than we found them.

That has been my motivation for the past 36 years in building Centaur Stride.

What began as a 4-H program in our backyard grew into a three-year journey of planning, building and overcoming obstacles before finally finding its home between Westfield and Sherman. After nearly a year of searching, we found the only property we could afford. We believed in the philosophy, "Build it and they will come." We were convinced that therapeutic horseback riding could make a meaningful difference in people’s lives, and we were determined to make it happen.

Friends rallied to help, challenges were overcome, and there was no turning back. When you care for live animals, the work doesn’t stop simply because people don’t show up. The horses still need feeding, care and attention. The bills still need paying. Success meant showing up every day, never giving up and finding a way to keep going.

For many years, the daily demands left little time to think about the future. Strategic planning, sustainability and long-term projections seemed distant luxuries when there was so much to accomplish just to get through another day.

Grants are not guaranteed. First, an organization must prove its worth. Then it must demonstrate a credible plan for sustainability. That requires knowledgeable, dedicated people who have the time to help build a future. The challenge is that we need funding to attract those people, but we need those people and their expertise to secure the funding.

Centaur Stride is finally getting closer to that goal, thanks to the people who care enough to help. But we cannot afford to pay the leadership needed to get us there, and without that leadership, securing the resources to sustain the organization becomes even more difficult.

GCFCU operates offices in Falconer, Dunkirk, Jamestown and Mayville. The credit union serves approximately 9,500 members, has roughly $100 million in assets, and employs about 30 staff members.

local.title: Fraternity pitches in at Greystone
local.summary: On a bright Saturday afternoon, members of the Delta Chi fraternity at SUNY Fredonia spent time giving back to the community by volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve. During a roadside cleanup, one fraternity brother made an unusual discovery: the body of a beautiful bird lying just off the main
local.body:
On a bright Saturday afternoon, members of the Delta Chi fraternity at SUNY Fredonia spent time giving back to the community by volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve.

During a roadside cleanup, one fraternity brother made an unusual discovery: the body of a beautiful bird lying just off the main road. The brothers named the bird "Mr. Tweetums" and brought it back to the nature preserve, where they held a mock funeral service in its honor. The bird was respectfully laid to rest beneath a beautiful white oak tree.

The brothers' gesture of respect and compassion for the deceased animal was a touching moment and perhaps an unexpected one for those who might not associate fraternity members with such a thoughtful tribute.

The visit to Greystone was an enjoyable experience for the brothers, who regularly participate in community service projects at the preserve. Bill Moran and Diane Clark welcomed the group by sharing their stories and experiences, teaching them about proper land preservation and providing fruit and snacks.

The afternoon also offered opportunities to share traditions and cultural experiences. Clark told the story of Persephone and the pomegranate, prompting one of the brothers, Ninyo, to share a Jewish tradition of eating pomegranates at the beginning of the new year as a symbol of the sweetness hoped for in the year ahead.

The fraternity members also enjoy helping Moran with various maintenance projects around the property. Their work includes turning over the raised garden beds to renew the soil and help preserve the beds for future use.

For the brothers of Delta Chi, volunteering at Greystone Nature Preserve is about more than completing a community service assignment. It provides genuine satisfaction in helping maintain an important piece of natural land while learning the value of conservation and hard work.

Although the projects can be physically demanding, the brothers have been reminded time and again that good things come to those willing to put in the effort.

local.title: Explosive water events blow up plan for district
local.summary: Fredonia’s recent conservation and boil water orders coupled with the explosive water main break on Johnson and Gardner streets highlight several very important facts critical for Fredonia water customers moving forward. First and foremost, the village’s infrastructure will need to be replaced no ma
local.body:
Fredonia's recent conservation and boil water orders coupled with the explosive water main break on Johnson and Gardner streets highlight several very important facts critical for Fredonia water customers moving forward. First and foremost, the village's infrastructure will need to be replaced no matter where the village draws their water from. Regardless of whether the village joins the North County Water District or continues to use their own gravity-fed system, ancient water mains will continue to burst and will continue to deliver discolored water to customers until the mains are replaced. And if the village is buying water from the NCWD, when those ancient water mains burst, as they will until they are replaced, Fredonia will pay for every drop of water lost. Why buy water from Dunkirk or the NCWD only to deliver it through old and corroded pipes and possibly lose large volumes of it by way of water main breaks?

The village's current $22 million plan to join the NCWD does not include the replacement of aging infrastructure. At a village board workshop a few months ago, the idea of adding an infrastructure replacement piece to the NCWD project was discussed. It was stated at the time that replacing some of the more decrepit water mains in the village would cost around $6 million. This idea bubble seemed to burst when the discussion turned to financing both the joining of the NCWD and the replacement of aged infrastructure. At the time it was stated by several key members of village government that the village could not afford to do both. With the NCWD project now paused due to a lack of funds, it would appear that the village cannot afford to join the NCWD anyway.

In October 2025, the village of Fredonia was placed under a water conservation order. Drought conditions had lowered Fredonia's reservoir to a concerning level. There were worries at the time that the village's reservoir would run dry and Fredonians would be left without water. The village has a pump station connected to the city of Dunkirk's water delivery system. This pump station was constructed so that the city and village could provide water to one another during water shortages and emergencies. But in October 2025 inquiring minds were told that the Vineyard Drive pump station couldn't be used as intended due to differences in water system pressure. There were also concerns about water compatibility. Fredonia adds the ion orthophosphate to their water in order to line ancient pipes and prevent metals from leaching into drinking water. In a decision that was widely criticized, the Vineyard Drive pump station was not used in the fall of 2025.

local.body:
The Fredonia Shakespeare Club met at the home of Ms. Susan Westling last week. Following a business meeting, the club heard Ms. Lucille Richardson's presentation on Amy Beach.

Amy Beach (1867 - 1944), formally known during her lifetime as Mrs. H.H.A. Beach, was America's first distinguished and celebrated woman composer of high art music. Overcoming Victorian conventions that largely restricted women to writing amateur parlor songs and teaching pieces, she became one of the first American composers of either gender to achieve international stature. Over her lifetime, she produced a prolific catalog of roughly 300 works. In addition to scores of songs, choral works and solo piano pieces, Beach composed numerous large-scale works. These included a mass, a symphony (the first composed and published by an American woman), a piano concerto, a violin sonata, a piano quintet, a trio, and a one-act opera.

Prodigiously gifted, her talent strikingly apparent almost from infancy, Beach began composing at age four and made her first public appearance as a pianist at age seven. At eighteen, she made her debut with the Boston Symphony Orchestra. That same year, she married a prominent Boston surgeon and yielded to his wish that she limit her public concertizing to focus on composition. Because she was denied formal composition instruction, Beach was self-taught as a composer by studying the works of European masters.

Following her husband's death in 1910, Beach traveled to Europe and achieved enormous success, performing her own works in major cultural centers. Upon returning to the United States just prior to World War I, she was greeted by enthusiastic public acclaim. A major milestone in her career was her fellowship appointment to the renowned MacDowell summer artists' colony in New Hampshire in 1921. Her twenty-year association with the latter inspired a shift in her compositional style, blending her signature lyricism with elements of impressionism and expressionism.

Beach lived and worked extensively in New York City during the final decades of her life. She became closely affiliated with St. Bartholomew's Episcopal Church where her choral compositions were frequently performed, making her a virtual composer-in-residence. Her works continued to be featured in other venues including the MET Orchestra Chamber Ensemble at Carnegie Hall.

Beach died in New York City at the age of 77 and is buried alongside her husband at Forest Hills Cemetery in Boston. Though her music endured a period of neglect after her death, it has experienced a major revival on the concert stage with about two-thirds of her total of 300 works now having been recorded.

local.body: The national ground stop may be over, but it could be some time before the aviation system gets back on track.At Buffalo Niagara International Airport, travelers told 7 News they were frustrated and uncertain about when they would finally be able to reach their destinations.An earlier nationwide ground stop threw travel plans into chaos, leaving passengers waiting for answers as delays and cancellations disrupted flights.For some, the uncertainty was enough to reconsider traveling altogether.Jim Rivera was headed to Atlanta to visit his daughter, but he said he would rather get a refund than risk traveling."Right now, we feel like we shouldn’t be traveling. What is going on in the air and on the ground is not safe to travel at this moment," Rivera said.Other passengers were dealing with missed connections and canceled plans.Ever Miranda said her flight to Fort Lauderdale was canceled. She was traveling for work and worried the disruption could cause her to miss her little sister’s birthday."I might miss my little sister’s birthday," Miranda said.Even after the ground stop was lifted, travelers were still waiting for updates and trying to figure out when they would get home.David Brown said he was growing frustrated with the uncertainty and did not even want to leave his spot in the airport because he feared getting stuck somewhere else."I am just going crazy here. I need to eat, and I don’t want to go inside yet because I don’t want to be stuck in one place," Brown said.Some travelers decided they did not want to wait any longer, turning to rental cars for another way home. For some, that meant facing more than 20 hours on the road.Adam Vanbrekel said driving offered more certainty than waiting for another flight.“I want to get back home, and then I know I’ll guarantee I make it there rather than guessing,” Vanbrekel said.Dylan Wood and his group also decided to drive rather than wait without knowing when they would be able to depart.“We didn't want to just sit and wait and not really have an answer on when we can actually depart, so just a group decision that we just decided to drive,” Wood said.WATCH: Ground stop lifted, but frustration lingers for travelers at Buffalo airportWhether waiting for a flight or hitting the road, travelers shared one common goal: getting home safely.While flights are beginning to resume, delays and cancellations may continue. entertainment.title: Despite Fallout, Billy Evans Would ‘100%’ Do ‘You Can See Everything’ Again
entertainment.summary: In first post-documentary interview, Elizabeth Holmes' husband tells CBS Sunday Morning why he always carries a gun and whether he plans to sue filmmakers
entertainment.body:
Elizabeth Holmes ’ husband Billy Evans sat down for his first televised interview since the release of You Can See Everything , the documentary that cast him in a negative light.

On CBS Sunday Morning , Evans tried to change the public’s perception about him in the aftermath of the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed film.

“I’m deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do,” Evans told CBS’s Matt Gutman. “But no, I am not some controlling monster who’s leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things.”

In previews ahead of Sunday’s interview , Evans talked about being a fan of You Can See Everything despite his villainous portrayal, as well as how he didn’t explicitly consent to his uncensored full-frontal shower scene.

With all the fallout from the movie, Evans was asked if he’d do it all again. “With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%,” Evans said. “Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into.”

In the latter half of the documentary, Evans revealed that he carries a firearm at all times, which concerned viewers as he is the caretaker of his young children with Holmes in prison. In the CBS interview, Evans explained why he’s always carrying.

“We have threats of violence against us daily,” he said. “I’ve got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.”

entertainment.title: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Unwraps $19M to Win Weekend in Box Office Return
entertainment.summary: Fellow newcomers 'Ghost Soldier' and 'How to Rob a Bank' are getting quieter starts over the weekend.
entertainment.body:
Ebenezer unwrapped $19 million domestically as star Johnny Depp ‘s studio comeback vehicle opened in first place at the domestic box office .

Paramount Pictures released director Ti West ‘s horror-tinged adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol in 3,535 North American theaters this weekend and landed an A- CinemaScore from audiences. Of the opening Thursday night audience, 62 percent of the crowd was over age 30, suggesting that the film was especially appealing for those who likely have positive associations with seeing Depp’s work throughout the decades. Ebenezer earned 4.5 out of 5 stars on PostTrak, with 50 percent of guests citing Depp as their reason for seeing the movie. Related Stories TV Billy Evans' First TV Interview to Air on 'CBS Sunday Morning': Where to Stream It Online Movies Christopher Abbott Reveals How His 'You Can See Everything' Moment Came to Be

It took in $23 million from international markets for a global start of $42 million.

Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Ian McKellen round out the cast for the $38 million-budgeted feature that stars Depp as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge who is visited by three spirits. Ebenezer marks Depp’s first studio project since 2018’s Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald , as he took a hiatus from high-profile work following abuse allegations from ex-wife Amber Heard that Depp has denied, in addition to negative headlines amid his and Heard’s 2022 defamation trial .

Paramount had been pleased with data suggesting that audiences want Depp back and that he still holds wide appeal, with the marketing including the actor appearing in character as Scrooge to remind fans of other transformative roles like Captain Jack Sparrow and Willy Wonka. Ebenezer has a PG-13 rating but is still geared toward the family crowd. Critics have been split on Ebenezer , as it holds a 53 percent approval rating from Rotten Tomatoes reviewers. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck declares that the film “fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.”

Among other new arrivals, Sony Pictures released Ghost Soldier in 2,558 North American locations on Wednesday, with director William Eubank’s action movie grossing around $5.2 million for the three-day frame and a $8.3 million domestic cume. Jim Caviezel plays a former Green Beret who must defend his Wyoming community against a corporate threat. Hailing from Mandalay Pictures, Ghost Soldier holds a 42 percent score from Rotten Tomatoes critics and a 90 percent from audiences.

entertainment.title: Michael J. Fox supported by wife Tracy Pollan and three daughters at actor’s Parkinson’s gala
entertainment.summary: The "Back to the Future" star founded the organization in 2000, nine years after he was diagnosed with Parkinson's.
entertainment.body:
Michael J. Fox stepped out with his wife, Tracy Pollan, and their three daughters to the actor’s 26th annual Parkinson’s gala.

The “Back to the Future” star attended his A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s event hosted at New York City’s Waldorf Astoria on Saturday.

Fox, 65, and Pollan, 66, beamed in coordinated black outfits as they posed with their daughters, 31-year-old twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, and Esmé, 25.

The star-studded event was founded by the actor in 2000, just nine years after he received his diagnosis at the age of 29. The gala raises money for research to find a cure for Parkinson’s disease.

“It’s all about the amazing work that the foundation has done. It celebrates everybody who’s worked with us for 20-plus years,” Pollan told People at the event Saturday.

“Just the huge and amazing amount of money that’s been raised that goes directly into the scientists’ pockets … We really are seeing so much progress,” she added.

The actress also reflected on Fox’s journey with Parkinson’s, telling the outlet, “You just have to do it day by day.”

“You have to look at what’s in front of you,” she explained. “And you have to stay in the moment — and if the moment is OK, that’s where you are.”

entertainment.title: Michael J. Fox Steps Out With All 3 Daughters for Rare Family Outing
entertainment.summary: Where Michael J. Fox is going, he just needs his family’s love. The Back to the Future star was not only joined by his wife Tracy Pollan for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s A Funny Thing Happened...
entertainment.body:
Where Michael J. Fox is going, he just needs his family’s love.

The Back to the Future star was not only joined by his wife Tracy Pollan for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s gala on Nov. 14, but also by three extra special guests.

When Fox and Pollan stepped out at the Waldorf Astoria in New York City for the fundraising event, they were accompanied by 31-year-old twins Aquinnah and Schuyler , as well as 25-year-old Esmé . The three girls each wore elegant gowns and big smiles as they posed on the event’s red carpet alongside their parents. (Fox and Pollan are also parents to 37-year-old son Sam , who was not in attendance.)

Pollan, for her part, donned a calf-length black shift dress and heels, while Fox wore a black blazer over a navy t-shirt and black slacks.

The gala featured performances from John Mayer and Brad Paisley , as well as comedy sets from Josh Johnson and Tom Papa , while actor Denis Leary helmed the night as emcee.

Fox started the Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000, nine years after he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. In the time since, the organization has become an important player in the fight to cure the disease—with the annual gala acting as a way to thank the many hands who make executing the mission light work.

As Pollan told People at the event, “It celebrates everybody who’s worked with us for 20-plus years. Just the huge and amazing amount of money that’s been raised that goes directly into the scientists’ pockets, and they can just do all the work that’s necessary [to finding a cure]. We really are seeing so much progress.”

The 66-year-old also shared insight into how she and her family navigate Fox’s health challenges.

entertainment.title: Matt Damon Reveals Ben Affleck’s Review of ‘The Odyssey’ — and the One Performance He Couldn’t Stop Talking About
entertainment.summary: Damon joined Tom Holland, John Leguizamo, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page for a conversation about Christopher Nolan's epic.
entertainment.body:
The Odyssey ‘s awards season campaign is in full swing, with Matt Damon , Tom Holland , John Leguizamo, Zendaya , Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page taking part in a screening event in Los Angeles on Saturday night.

The group united for a 40-minute Q&A to discuss their experience on Christopher Nolan’s hit film , while also paying plenty of compliments to each others’ performances. And though he wasn’t in attendance, Robert Pattinson stole the show, as Damon revealed that “ Ben Affleck probably talked to me for 20 minutes about just Rob after he saw the movie.” Related Stories Movies Robert Downey Jr. Interviews Christopher Nolan, Matt Damon About 'The Odyssey' (Exclusive Video) Movies Santa Barbara Film Fest: Anne Hathaway, Star of 'The Odyssey,' Tapped for American Riviera Award

“When they talk about a brave performance — Ben goes, ‘You had the benefit of all of the might and power of Christopher Nolan storytelling at your back’ and I went, ‘Yeah’ and he goes, ‘Rob had all of the weight and heft and power of Christopher Nolan’s storytelling coming down on him. And the way he did it, it was like watching a guy run into an avalanche,'” Damon told the crowd at the Academy Museum. “Any moment that he could be more cowardly, more hateable, you could see his wheels turning. ‘How could I make this even worse for myself?’ And it was so fun to watch because he’s such a dynamic actor and so interesting.”

There was also plenty of praise for Damon himself, as the cast noted how much the star had to go through physically and emotionally to play the role of Odysseus.

Patel recalled how one day when they were shooting some brutal scenes on the seas, “A bunch of the guys on the boat, they were they were starting to like flag, and Matt turned around to us and he said, ‘I know this is hard, but how many actors are in SAG? Every single one of them would die to be where you are right now.’ And we were like, ‘Well, we can’t argue with that.’ I mean, that’s completely true. Shut up, get on with it,” adding that even during the taxing moments, Damon would be “smiling, happy, just loving it.”

Holland shouted out the scene between Damon and Anne Hathaway when Odysseus has returned to Ithaca but is still in hiding, saying he wasn’t supposed to be on set that day but wanted to come see the actors in action.

“Watching you guys go the distance in that scene just really set the tone for us of the level that we should all aspire to be at for a movie like this,” Holland said. “I couldn’t do that yet. I need a few more years.”

entertainment.title: Marvel Star Sebastian Stan Played A Disney Character In A Hit ABC Fantasy Series
entertainment.summary: Before he became a staple of the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Bucky Barnes, Sebastian Stan played an interesting role on a fantastical ABC show.
entertainment.body:
Chuck Zlotnick/Marvel Studios Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Sebastian Stan started out by playing Captain America's best friend, Bucky Barnes. In the 15 years since the character's onscreen debut in 2011, the Winter Soldier has become a fan favorite and a hero of his own. But when Stan's MCU narrative was still in its infancy, he was immersed in the fairytale world of the ABC fantasy series "Once Upon a Time" playing another character with a tortured mind, the Mad Hatter.

"Once Upon a Time" is set in the fictitious Storybrooke, Maine, where fairytale fantasies meet modern reality due to a curse. Stan's part as the Mad Hatter, whose civilian name is Jefferson, was a guest-starring role. His rendition of the classic fairytale character from Lewis Carroll's "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" made his first appearance in Season 1, released in 2011, while his last appearance came in Season 2.

In a 2014 interview with Zap2it , Stan reminisced on his time as the Mad Hatter while doing press for "Captain America: The Winter Soldier." He spoke of the fun he had with the character and the potential for where its storyline could go. "There's so many possibilities there," Stan said of the Mad Hatter/Jefferson. "One of the things those guys did so well — out of the many things — is they just reinvented all of those characters in a new way. They reintroduced them to a whole new generation. The Mad Hatter was never like that in just the cartoon. It remains to be seen."

ABC/YouTube While Sebastian Stan only appeared in the first two seasons of "Once Upon a Time," the hit fantasy TV show aired on ABC for seven total seasons. It also had a 13-episode spin-off, "Once Upon a Time in Wonderland," which was meant to feature Stan reprising his role as the Mad Hatter. But Stan's time in that fairytale universe coincided with Bucky's growing role in the MCU.

When speaking with Zap2it in 2014, Stan already mentioned that coming back to "Once Upon a Time" wasn't "really on (his) radar." When the Marvel star made such comments, "Once Upon a Time" co-creators Adam Horowitz and Edward Kitsis were already aware that Stan might be too busy to return. "We love Sebastian and we are probably the heads of the Sebastian Stan fan club, but he's in demand," Kitsis said in a 2013 interview with E! News . "We're not the only ones that love him! Unfortunately, his schedule is nonstop."

entertainment.title: 10 Most Disappointing Netflix Series Cancellations, Ranked
entertainment.summary: Netflix has earned a notorious reputation for pulling the plug on fan-favorite TV shows, and these are the cancellations that hurt us the most.
entertainment.body:
Netflix Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Nobody cancels a show quite like Netflix. Especially during the streamer's ascendancy in the mid- to late 2010s, fans and commentators alike would talk about its programming decisions as if it were the first ever to axe a beloved show. Of course, this wasn't true — but we understand why it felt that way.

Hidden viewership data, confusing public messaging (oh, the many reversed renewals), and a sea of largely interchangeable "content" essentially made it so that, gradually, it was near-impossible to predict (or understand with hindsight) these decisions outside one's personalized content algorithm. Sometimes, a show would only seem popular to you because everyone on your feed was talking about it. It's hardly surprising that, in this context, cancellations felt more personal too.

Regardless of whether the shows below were secretly ratings disasters, budget drags, or some combination of the two, their premature endings sparked extraordinary backlash from fans. Viewers signed petitions and paid for billboards in Times Square just for one extra hour of these mostly forgotten series. Worst of all, because many of the shows' writers embraced that old TV hack of ending a season on a cliffhanger to stir interest in a renewal, some of these incredible shows are only debatably worth watching given that they end in the middle of their stories.

"Inside Job" is but one of a disappointing number of Netflix series canceled after already receiving a public renewal order. Created by Shion Takeuchi and executive produced by Alex Hirsch ("Gravity Falls"), this adult animated conspiracy comedy imagines a secret, high-tech, paranormal-adjacent bureaucracy responsible for keeping the world in order. Lizzy Caplan and Clark Duke voice the leading characters, with Christian Slater supporting. It was part of the early wave of Netflix adult animated series, which also included "Q-Force" and "The Midnight Gospel" — neither of which made it past one season.

"Inside Job" met the same fate, despite being greenlit for Season 2 roughly seven months before its cancellation. That winter 2022–2023 period also saw Netflix axe "Warrior Nun," Mike Flanagan's "The Midnight Club," and the "Dark" successor "1899," all of which had solid fanbases behind them. Official explanations were not provided, though staff writer Chase Mitchell (who actually broke the news in a series of deleted tweets, via PopCulture ) accused Netflix of not caring about animated series. Takeuchi was only slightly more diplomatic in her official statement, openly stating that the story deserved more time.

entertainment.title: 5 Dark Facts Every NCIS Fan Needs To Know About Mark Harmon's Gibbs

entertainment.body:

Since 2003, audiences have peered into the unique, technical world of naval special investigations. At the forefront of the journey was Leroy Jethro Gibbs (Mark Harmon), the silver-haired supervisor of the Washington D.C. NCIS Major Case Response Team. Between his trademark personal set of rules and his loyalty to the job, Gibbs is both a dedicated leader and a mentor to his team. But throughout 18 seasons, audiences were presented with details and instances of his life that showcased some darker aspects of his character.

Between his tragic background and his own regretful actions, Gibbs is not without demons. But these demons and experiences shaped him into the man he is — and helped him become the character audiences love. Any NCIS fan who has followed Gibbs since the first season should know these five dark, unsettling facts about him.

CBS Gibbs has been married four times, and the last three all ended in divorce. But the end to his first marriage was owed to much more tragic circumstances. His wife Shannon (Darby Stanchfield) and eight-year-old daughter Kelly (Mary Mouser) were murdered by cartel member Pedro Hernandez (Thomas Rosales Jr.). While Gibbs was fighting overseas in Operation Desert Storm, Shannon witnessed Hernandez kill a Marine sergeant from Camp Pendleton and agreed to testify against him in court.

Before the court proceedings, they were being driven to a safehouse when Hernandez, armed with a sniper rifle, fired a round into the driver's head. The car crashed, killing Shannon and Kelly. Upon learning of his family's slaying, and being unable to attend the funeral, Gibbs tried to commit suicide by walking directly into enemy fire during an engagement. He survived, but was in a coma for days. And this self-destructive behavior continued, with it being the depressing reason why Gibbs never locks his front door .

CBS Despite losing his first wife, Gibbs would try to find love again. At one point, he became engaged to fellow Marine Ellen Wallace (Erin Cummings). In 2001, Ellen started digging into a coverup regarding a 1998 military operation in Kosovo. Daniel Kent (Doug Savant), another Marine, killed her to hide his involvement in the coverup. The murder took place on September 10, 2001, and for years it was believed that she was a victim of the 9/11 terrorist attacks on The Pentagon.
